- [ ] **Step 2: Parse the TCF v2 string** if present. Read from
      `req.user.consent` **only** — the normalized OpenRTB 2.6 field.
      Legacy `user.ext.consent` is rejected by the ingest gate at
      [checks.rs:46](../../../crates/auctioneer-openrtb/src/prepare/checks.rs#L46),
      so by the time `resolve` runs the only place a TCF string can
      live is the normalized field.

  **Step 2.0 — GPP section-2 authoritative-source guard (round-75 B1 —
  FAIL CLOSED; this is a BEHAVIOURAL rule, not just a release-label
  note).** Per §7.4, when `regs.gpp_sid` contains **section 2**, GPP
  section 2 (TCFEU2) is the AUTHORITATIVE GDPR consent source and WINS
  over `user.consent`. GDPR enforcement has no GPP decoder, so it cannot read that
  authoritative source. Therefore: **if `gpp_sid` contains section 2,
  set `consent_usable = false` and do NOT read `user.consent` at all**
  — skip the three-way split below. This covers the dangerous MIXED /
  CONFLICTING case the round-72 note missed: a request with a STALE
  legacy `user.consent` that GRANTS plus an authoritative
  `regs.gpp` section-2 that DENIES would otherwise be granted by
  reading `user.consent` (a fail-OPEN privacy violation). Failing
  closed on ANY active section-2 request — GPP-only, mixed, or
  conflicting — is the only safe GDPR enforcement behaviour until privacy enforcement lands the
  TCFEU2 extractor + conflict handling. (A section-2 `gpp_sid` with an
  absent/empty `regs.gpp` is likewise undecodable → also
  `consent_usable = false`; the existing `regs_gpp_conflict` warning
  still fires for the signal mismatch.) Only when `gpp_sid` does NOT
  contain section 2 does the resolver reach the `user.consent` ladder
  below.

  **What `consent_usable = false` means here — round-76 B2 (precise;
  it is NOT "deny all traffic").** The section-2 guard routes through
  the SAME unusable-consent path as empty/malformed/GVL-unavailable
  consent, so `permissions()` returns the standard `default_permissions()`
  row: **`{ AllowBidRequest: !P2_enforced, PassGeo: !SF1_enforced,
PassID: false }`**. The guarantee that actually closes the round-75 B1
  fail-open is **`PassID: false` unconditionally** — the ignored
  (possibly-stale) `user.consent` can never grant an ID. `AllowBidRequest`
  / `PassGeo` are denied only _to the extent the operator ENFORCES_
  purpose 2 / special feature 1; with enforcement off, bid/geo still
  flow (the operator's configured choice, consistent with every other
  consent path). And this row is reached ONLY on the enforcement path:
  a request that is out of scope — `enforcement_active == false` via the
  host master kill-switch, a non-standard-publisher account, a
  not-enabled channel, or `Signal::No` — takes the
  `allow_all_no_scrub()` branch BEFORE `permissions()` and is allow-all
  regardless of `gpp_sid`. So the correct claim is "section-2 consent is
  treated as unusable → `default_permissions()` (no ID, and no bid/geo
  where enforced)," NOT "all section-2 traffic is denied."

  **Three-way split on the consent value** (reached only when GPP
  section 2 is NOT in scope, per Step 2.0) (spec Appendix E line
  5054 — empty consent is NOT a request error, only malformed
  consent is). Round-52 Critical: each unusable branch sets
  `consent_usable = false`, so `permissions()` returns the A.4
  default row directly (no A.2/A.3 walk):
  1. `None` (field absent) → `consent_usable = false`. No warning.
  2. `Some("")` (present-but-empty) → `consent_usable = false`.
     **No warning.** Empty-string consent is the "no opt-in
     collected yet" convention; it's not malformed.
  3. `Some(s)` with a non-empty `s` → feed into `parse_tcf_v2`.
     On parse failure, append an `InvalidPrivacyConsent` warning
     via Task 7's `malformed_tcf(err)` constructor
     (`scope: "user.consent"`) and set `consent_usable = false`
     (treat as no-consent). On success, proceed to GVL selection;
     `consent_usable` becomes `true` only if that GVL is found.

  **Round-53 H2 — how the unusable branches build the FULL
  context.** All three unusable branches (and the GVL-unavailable
  branch) build the context through ONE constructor, so every
  field is populated even though `permissions()` won't consult the
  consent-dependent ones. `per_purpose_effective` (and the derived
  `p2_enforced`/`sf1_enforced`) are computed from CONFIG in Step 3
  BEFORE the consent split, so they are always available; `tcf` is
  `None` (or the failed-parse remnant is discarded), `gvl` is
  `Gvl::empty()`, `alias_gvl_ids` is still read from the request:

  ```rust
  // Round-54 H1: every enforcement value is passed EXPLICITLY (no
  // undefined helper, no comment-valued field), and the literal
  // lists ALL of PrivacyContext's fields (the auction core stub had none —
  // the "existing auction core fields" comment on the struct is a leftover
  // and is removed). `p2_enforced`/`sf1_enforced`/`sf1_effective`
  // are computed ONCE in Step 3 and threaded to both this path and
  // the success path.
  fn enforced_but_empty(
      per_purpose_effective: BTreeMap<u8, PurposeEnforcement>,
      p2_enforced: bool,
      sf1_enforced: bool,
      sf1_effective: Option<SpecialFeatureEnforcement>,
      alias_gvl_ids: BTreeMap<Box<str>, u32>,
      basic_enforcement_vendors: BTreeSet<String>,
      warnings: Vec<NonFatalWarning>,
  ) -> PrivacyContext {
      PrivacyContext {
          warnings,
          per_purpose_effective,
          consent_usable: false,
          p2_enforced,
          sf1_enforced,
          tcf: None,
          gvl: Gvl::empty(),
          alias_gvl_ids,
          basic_enforcement_vendors,
          sf1_effective,
      }
  }
  ```

  The `Some(gvl)` success path calls the SAME builder shape (or a
  sibling that sets `consent_usable: true`, `tcf: Some(parsed)`,
  `gvl: found`) with the identical `p2_enforced`/`sf1_enforced`/
  `sf1_effective`/`alias_gvl_ids`/`basic_enforcement_vendors`. Every
  field is listed in both, so none is left unpopulated.

  **Ordering (round-54 H1).** Step 3 (build `per_purpose_effective`
  - resolve `sf1_effective`, and derive `p2_enforced =
per_purpose_effective.get(&2).map_or(false, |e| e.enforce_purpose ==
TriState::Enabled)` and `sf1_enforced =
sf1_effective.as_ref().map_or(false, |e| e.enforce ==
TriState::Enabled)` — both plain field reads, no new method) runs
    BEFORE the Step 2 consent split in the
    executable resolver body, even though it is written as "Step 3":
    the step numbers are exposition order, and the resolver computes
    the config-derived enforcement first because it is
    consent-independent. Both the usable and unusable branches then
    consume those already-computed values.

  **GPP TCFEU2 (section 2) decoding is deferred to privacy enforcement; GDPR enforcement FAILS CLOSED
  on every active section-2 request (round-75 B1 — supersedes the
  round-72 "GPP-only" framing, which was wrong).** Spec §7.4 / Appendix
  D.1 make GPP section 2 the AUTHORITATIVE GDPR consent source that WINS
  over `user.consent` when present. GDPR enforcement has no GPP decoder. The round-72
  note claimed the only affected case was "GPP-only" traffic and that
  GDPR enforcement was therefore always SAFE (over-restrictive). **That was false:**
  GDPR enforcement's ladder read `user.consent` unconditionally, so a request with a
  stale legacy `user.consent` that GRANTS _plus_ an authoritative
  `regs.gpp` section-2 that DENIES would be GRANTED — a fail-OPEN
  privacy violation, exactly the mixed/conflicting case "GPP-only"
  excluded. The corrected behaviour (Step 2.0 above): **whenever
  `gpp_sid` contains section 2, GDPR enforcement ignores `user.consent` and marks
  consent UNUSABLE (`consent_usable = false`).** This covers GPP-only,
  mixed, AND conflicting signals — GDPR enforcement never trusts a legacy consent an
  authoritative-but-undecodable GPP could override. **Production
  boundary (round-76 B2 — precise):** the GDPR enforcement release label states that
  **section-2 GDPR consent is treated as UNUSABLE → the
  `default_permissions()` row (`PassID: false` unconditionally; bid/geo
  denied where P2/SF1 are enforced), on the enforcement path only** —
  NOT that "all section-2 traffic is denied" (out-of-scope /
  `enforcement_active == false` requests are allow-all and never reach
  this row) and NOT that "GPP-only traffic is excluded" (the round-72
  framing). The privacy guarantee is that no ID leaks from a stale
  legacy consent; honouring (rather than nullifying) section-2 consent
  is privacy enforcement. Regression tests:
  `gpp_sid_section2_with_granting_user_consent_yields_passid_false()`
  (the fail-open guard — asserts `PassID: false` despite a granting
  `user.consent`) and `gpp_sid_without_section2_reads_user_consent()`
  (the legacy path is unaffected).

      **Purpose-id set = union** of `host.gdpr.tcf2.purposes.keys()`
      and `account.gdpr.purposes.keys()` (both are the concrete
      `BTreeMap<u8, PurposeEnforcement>` type on `Tcf2Config` /
      `AccountGdprConfig` per Task 2 — the `Option`-wrapping in Task
      15's `AccountOverride` is a boot-time-only overlay shape; by the

  **Per-field merge — spec-compliant.** Spec §9 line 3889
  enumerates the ONLY tri-state fields that cross the host/account
  boundary: GDPR per-purpose `enforce_purpose` / `enforce_vendors`,
  `gdpr.channel_enabled`, `gdpr.enabled`, `ccpa.channel_enabled`.
  Round-87 B2: `allow_li_transparency` is no longer a config field at
  all — it is a per-call invocation override on the A.3 row-5 path
  (Task 6 Step 2), so it does not appear in this merge. `enforce_algo`
  and `vendor_exceptions` remain account-only.
  Same rule for the SF1 fields (Task 9's `PassGeo` derivation
  reads `account.gdpr.special_features` when present, else
  `host.gdpr.tcf2.special_features` — that's SF1's own
  independent resolver, NOT a per-field tri-state fallthrough on
  a shared struct):

  ```rust
  fn effective_purpose(host: &PurposeEnforcement,
                       acct: Option<&PurposeEnforcement>)
      -> PurposeEnforcement
  {
      let Some(acct) = acct else { return host.clone(); };
      PurposeEnforcement {
          // account-only fields per spec §9:3889 (not in the
          // exhaustive tri-state fallthrough list)
          enforce_algo:          acct.enforce_algo,
          vendor_exceptions:     acct.vendor_exceptions.clone(),

          // Only the two tri-state fields §9:3889 authorises for
          // host fallthrough
          enforce_purpose: tri_or(acct.enforce_purpose, host.enforce_purpose),
          enforce_vendors: tri_or(acct.enforce_vendors, host.enforce_vendors),
      }
  }

  fn tri_or(a: TriState, h: TriState) -> TriState {
      if a == TriState::Unset { h } else { a }
  }
  ```

  Whole-map replacement of the host purposes by the account is
  explicitly NOT the semantics — an account that overrides purpose
  3 only leaves the other 9 purposes at their host values. See
  Task 15 "Overlay semantics" for the boot-time overlay path that
  produces this concrete `AccountConfig` shape.
  Cache into `PrivacyContext.per_purpose_effective:
BTreeMap<u8, PurposeEnforcement>` — an owned copy so
  `PrivacyContext` needs no lifetime.

      The GVL vendor map is keyed by `u16`. The resolution + narrowing
      rules:

  2. Else look up `auctioneer_config::bidder(core_name).
and_then(|b| b.gvl_vendor_id)`.
  3. **Boundary + zero handling** (round-25 H1 rewrite — earlier

     just normalizes to 0 when absent):

0`** and continue into the first-match table. Under A.2

       and match the wrong vendor. Explicit handling

u16::MAX"))` for any entry with `id > u16::MAX as

!p2_enforced` can be true, which is not the required full deny.)

- [ ] **Step 2: Build `AuctionPermissions`** by dispatching each
      gate through Task 6's effective algorithm. Per-permission wiring:
  - `AllowBidRequest` = purpose 2 effective legal basis.
    **Dispatch through `purpose_effective_algo(ctx, 2, core)` with the
    CONFIGURED per-purpose flags** (not forced — forced flags are the
    PassID pass, not the auction-side "may this bidder bid" pass;
    round-87 B3 — `core` only, no alias). Bidders in

    enforcement here would deny basic bidders any bid permission
    even when their basic legal basis passes.
    ```rust

    // round-87 B2: allow_li_transparency = true ONLY here (basic P2).
    let allow_bid_request = match purpose_effective_algo(ctx, 2, core) {
        EnforceAlgo::Basic => purpose_allowed_basic(ctx, 2, core, vendor_id, p2_flags, /* allow_li_transparency */ true),
        EnforceAlgo::Full  => purpose_allowed(ctx, 2, core, vendor_id, p2_flags),
    };
    ```
    The `effective_flags_for_purpose(ctx, p)` helper reads
    `ctx.per_purpose_effective.get(&p)` (Task 8 Step 3's cached
    table) and returns the resolved `EnforceFlags`. When the
    purpose is NOT in the map (host + account both declared no
    opinion — reachable whenever the operator's TOML doesn't
    enumerate every purpose id 1..=10), the helper returns
    `EnforceFlags { enforce_purpose: false, enforce_vendors: false }`
    per the default-permissions rule. This is the sparse-map
    safety fence — direct `[&p]` indexing would panic on a
    Task-19-style config that only configures purpose 2. Same
    helper is used by `PassGeo` (below) and `PassID` (Step 2's
    PassID paragraph, which walks p ∈ 2..=10 unconditionally).
  - `PassGeo` reads SF1 enforcement from Task 2's SF1 config
    (`account.gdpr.special_features.get(&1)` falling back to
    `host.gdpr.tcf2.special_features.get(&1)` via the same
    account→host resolver used for purposes). Let
    `sf1_enforced = matches!(sf1.enforce, TriState::Enabled)` and
    `sf1_vendor_exceptions` be the effective exception list from
    that config entry (empty when SF1 is unconfigured).
    `PassGeo` requires ALL of:
    1. Special-feature 1 is opt-in on the TCF string
       (`tcf.special_feature_optins.contains(&1)`), OR
       `!sf1_enforced`, OR `core_name` (the CORE bidder — the alias
       name is NEVER consulted per round-87 B3) is listed in
       `sf1_vendor_exceptions`.
    2. The vendor declares SF1 in its GVL entry
       (`gvl.vendor(vendor_id).map_or(false, |v| v.special_features

       A false result on any of these denies `PassGeo`. When SF1 is

false` — the default is to permit `PassGeo` per the

  - `PassID` = OR over the **effective** legal-basis algorithm for

    Implementation:
    ```rust

    // round-87 B2: allow_li_transparency = (p == 2) — ONLY basic P2 may

    let pass_id = (2u8..=10u8).any(|p| {
    ```

    Any single satisfied purpose in `2..=10` under this forced-

    - A.3 basic enforcement "never consults the GVL declaration
      set" at all (Step 2).
      So a bidder in `vendor_exceptions` or `basic_enforcement_vendors`
      would get some purpose in 2..=10 = `true` → `PassID = true`,
      directly contradicting Appendix A.4 (empty/malformed/GVL-fail →
      `PassID = false`). An empty GVL relocates the fail-open, it does
      not close it. The ONLY correct fix is an explicit
      unusable-consent state that returns the deterministic row
      before exceptions or legal-basis evaluation.

    **Mechanism.** `PrivacyContext` carries `consent_usable: bool`
    (set in `resolve` — see below). `permissions(core, bidder)`:

    ```rust
    pub fn permissions(&self, core: &str, bidder: &str) -> AuctionPermissions {
        if !self.consent_usable {
            // Appendix A.4 empty/malformed/GVL-fail row. Deterministic,
            // per-request (NOT per-bidder): no vendor_exceptions, no
            // basic-enforcement, no GVL, no TCF consulted.
            return self.default_permissions_row();
        }
        // ... the normal per-bidder A.2/A.3 walk (Step 1/Step 2) ...
    }

    fn default_permissions_row(&self) -> AuctionPermissions {
        AuctionPermissions::Partial {
            allow_bid_request: !self.p2_enforced,   // resolved P2 enforce_purpose
            pass_geo:          !self.sf1_enforced,  // resolved SF1 enforcement
            pass_id:           false,               // ALWAYS false on unusable consent
        }
    }
    ```

    `p2_enforced` / `sf1_enforced` are the request-level resolved
    enforcement booleans (from `per_purpose_effective[2]` and the
    SF1 config), cached on the context at resolve time. `resolve`
    sets `consent_usable = false` for the empty/absent-consent path
    (Step 2 case 1/2), the malformed-parse path (Step 2 case 3
    failure), AND the GVL-unavailable path; `true` ONLY when a valid
    TCF parsed AND its `(spec, list)` GVL was found.

  Do NOT return the default row from the fully-non-enforced path.
  Out-of-scope traffic must reach `AllowAll`, not `{PassID: false}`.

      bidder.

- **Create: `crates/auctioneer-core/src/host_primitives/race.rs`**
  — round-34 B1 moved forward from Task 11. **Round-53 B5 — the
  full implementation, not a name.** `BiasedRace3` is a runtime-
  neutral three-arm biased race (no `tokio::select!`, so it
  compiles for wasm). It polls its arms in slice order, so on the
  same wake the EARLIER arm wins — this is what makes the
  `equal_call_timeout_and_deadline_ties_to_bidder_cause` guarantee
  hold (bidder arm indexed before deadline arm).

  **Round-54 B3 — the race OWNS its arms (`Pin<Box<dyn Future>>`),
  so dropping the race cancels the losers.** The round-53 draft
  stored `Pin<&'a mut dyn Future>` (BORROWED); dropping the race
  would then drop only the references, not the futures — the
  caller's `pin!` bindings still own them, so no cancellation
  happens and `pending_arms_are_dropped_on_completion` could not
  pass. Owning boxed futures fixes it: dropping `BiasedRace3` (or
  the whole `drive_one` frame when it returns) drops the two losing
  futures, cancelling the in-flight `send` (round-31 B2 transport
  cancellation). Three small box allocations per bidder call is
  negligible against a network round-trip.

  ```rust
  use core::future::Future;
  use core::pin::Pin;
  use core::task::{Context, Poll};
  // Round-55 B3: `Box` is in the std prelude — no `use` needed. The
  // round-54 `use alloc::boxed::Box;` fails with E0433 because
  // `auctioneer-core` is a std crate with no `extern crate alloc`.

  /// Polls `arms[0]`, then `arms[1]`, then `arms[2]` on every wake;
  /// returns the first `Ready`. Earlier index wins a simultaneous
  /// wake (biased). OWNS the three futures — dropping `self` drops
  /// the losers → cancellation.
  pub struct BiasedRace3<'a, T> {
      arms: [Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + 'a>>; 3],
  }

  impl<'a, T> BiasedRace3<'a, T> {
      pub fn new(
          a: impl Future<Output = T> + 'a,
          b: impl Future<Output = T> + 'a,
          c: impl Future<Output = T> + 'a,
      ) -> Self {
          Self { arms: [Box::pin(a), Box::pin(b), Box::pin(c)] }
      }
  }

  impl<T> Future for BiasedRace3<'_, T> {
      type Output = T;
      fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<T> {
          for arm in self.arms.iter_mut() {
              if let Poll::Ready(v) = arm.as_mut().poll(cx) {
                  return Poll::Ready(v);   // the other two arms drop
                                           // when `self` drops after await
              }
          }
          Poll::Pending
      }
  }
  ```

  The `new(a, b, c)` signature now takes the futures BY VALUE
  (`impl Future`), so the caller no longer `pin!`s them — see the
  updated `drive_one` call site (round-54 B3).
  Cancellation tests (in `race.rs`, `futures::executor::block_on`):
  - `earlier_arm_wins_on_simultaneous_ready()` — three arms all
    `Ready` on first poll; asserts arm 0's value is returned.
  - `pending_arms_are_dropped_on_completion()` — arms 1 and 2 hold
    a `DropFlag`; when arm 0 completes and the race is dropped,
    both flags flipped (losing futures cancelled).
  - `waits_for_first_ready()` — arms 0/1 `Pending`, arm 2 `Ready`;
    returns arm 2's value.

  `ProxyClientApi::send_one` becomes

  ```rust
  fn classify(
      outcome: Result<BidderHttpResponse, ProxyError>,
      max_response_bytes: usize,
  ) -> Result<BidderHttpResponse, FanoutError> {
      match outcome {
          Ok(resp) if resp.body.len() > max_response_bytes =>
              Err(FanoutError::OversizeResponse),         // post-buffer, (4,100)
          Ok(resp) if resp.status >= 500 =>
              Err(FanoutError::BadServerResponse),
          Ok(resp) => Ok(resp),
          // Round-52 H1 — the untrusted transport string is NEVER
          // logged. It goes NOWHERE: not the wire (public_message),
          // not the log (category only). A blocklist scrub is
          // bypassable (standalone `token=xyz`, non-URL kv); the
          // only safe rule is to log allowlisted metadata — here,
          // the fixed CATEGORY — and drop the free text entirely.
          Err(ProxyError::Transport(_detail)) => {
              log::warn!(target: "auctioneer::fanout", "bidder transport error");
              // Carry a FIXED string, not the raw detail, so even a
              // stray `{:?}` on the FanoutError cannot leak.
              Err(FanoutError::Other("transport error".to_owned()))
          }
      }
  }
  ```

  **Round-52 H1 — allowlist, not blocklist.** The round-51 draft
  `redact_transport_detail` was a blocklist (strip `user:pw@` and
  `?query` from URL-shaped whitespace tokens). A blocklist misses
  everything not shaped like a URL: a standalone `token=xyz`, a
  bearer credential, an `Authorization: …` fragment, or any
  key/value the upstream error happens to include. It is REMOVED.
  The untrusted `ProxyError::Transport(String)` is logged as the
  fixed category only; its bytes reach neither a log sink nor the
  wire. **Round-54 auction core — no bidder-name is logged here.** The
  round-52 note promised a `log::warn!("bidder {} …", name)`, but

  — `{ request, timeout, max_response_bytes, endpoint_compression }`),
  so there is no `name` in scope. The promise is REMOVED rather
  than plumbing a name through (and raw request aliases must never
  be logged anyway). If per-bidder attribution is wanted later,
  add a baked, sanitized `core_name: BidderName` to `BidderCall`
  in a dedicated change — out of scope for GDPR fanout. Wire safety is
  unchanged from round-51 H4: `run.rs` uses `public_message()`

  ```rust
              FanoutError::Unreachable      => "bidder unreachable",
              FanoutError::BadServerResponse => "bidder server error",
              FanoutError::OversizeResponse => "bidder response too large",
  ```

  GDPR fanout's `ProxyError` is the error type of the BUFFERED `send_one`

- [ ] **Step 1 — Add the `Timer` trait.**

  ```rust
  #[async_trait(?Send)]
  pub trait Timer: Send + Sync {
      /// Sleep for the given duration. Callers compute
      /// `duration = deadline_at.saturating_sub(clock.now_monotonic())`
      /// AT CALL TIME. Round-24 C3: the previous
      /// `sleep_until(deadline: Duration)` API was ambiguous
      /// because the epoch of `Duration` is impl-defined —
      /// `SystemClock`'s monotonic is a per-process anchor
      /// initialised on first call, while `tokio::time::Instant`
      /// has its own epoch. `sleep(Duration)` lifts the epoch
      /// question out of the trait; each impl converts to its
      /// runtime primitive directly (Axum:
      /// `tokio::time::sleep`; wasm stubs: immediate `Ready`).
      async fn sleep(&self, duration: Duration);
  }
  ```

- [ ] **Step 2 — Add `Timer for FakeClock` with waker registry.**
      Round-27 H6: the earlier "spelled out in Task 11" reference was
      incorrect — Task 11 held no such spec. Full algorithm follows.

  **Shape:**

  ```rust
  // crates/auctioneer-runtime/src/fake_clock.rs additions
  use std::collections::BTreeMap;
  use std::future::Future;
  use std::pin::Pin;
  use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
  use std::task::{Context, Poll, Waker};
  use std::time::Duration;

  struct FakeClockInner {
      now: Duration,               // monotonic, only ever advanced
      next_waiter_id: u64,
      waiters: BTreeMap<u64, Waiter>,
  }

  struct Waiter {
      wake_at: Duration,
      waker: Waker,
  }

  pub struct FakeClock {
      inner: Arc<Mutex<FakeClockInner>>,
      wall: OffsetDateTime,
  }
  ```

  **Trait impl** (algorithm — one operation per bullet, wake-
  outside-lock discipline strict):

  1. `Timer::sleep(&self, duration)` returns a custom
     `SleepFuture` handle owned by the caller. The handle
     carries `Arc<Mutex<FakeClockInner>>`, a `wake_at:
Duration`, and an `Option<u64>` waiter id (`None` until
     first poll).
  2. **Zero-duration** — the trait method computes
     **`wake_at = now.saturating_add(duration)`** (round-28 H1:
     earlier `now + duration` panics on
     `sleep(Duration::MAX)` once `now` is nonzero — `Duration`
     addition panics on overflow. Saturating add produces
     `Duration::MAX` as the effectively-forever wake instant
     and lets `advance_to(Duration::MAX)` drain deterministically
     without a panic). If `duration.is_zero()`, the returned
     future is `std::future::ready(())` (round-27 H6: never
     enters the waiter registry, no lock contention on the fast
     path).
  3. **Registration on first poll:** `SleepFuture::poll`
     acquires the mutex, checks `now >= wake_at` under the
     lock, and:
     - If already elapsed → set `state = Done`, release lock,
       return `Poll::Ready(())`.
     - Otherwise → mint `waiter_id = inner.next_waiter_id`
       followed by an increment guarded by `#[expect]`:
       ```rust
       #[expect(
           clippy::expect_used,
           reason = "u64 waiter id overflow requires 2^64 registrations in one FakeClock lifetime — treating it as a workspace-invariant panic is safer than silently wrapping and colliding waiter identities"
       )]
       {
           inner.next_waiter_id = inner
               .next_waiter_id
               .checked_add(1)
               .expect("waiter id overflow");
       }
       ```
       (Round-32 auction core: the `#[expect(...)]` annotation is required
       under the workspace restriction gate. `u64` overflow takes
       ~2^64 registrations — deliberately unreachable.)
       insert `Waiter { wake_at, waker: cx.waker().clone() }`
       into `waiters`, remember `Some(waiter_id)` in the
       future state, release lock, return `Poll::Pending`.
  4. **Repoll (waker replacement):** subsequent polls
     re-acquire the lock, look up the stored `waiter_id`, and
     if present replace `waker` via `Waker::clone_from` iff
     `!existing.will_wake(cx.waker())` (avoids the
     unnecessary drop-clone-store dance on the same waker).
     A repoll after the wake step is treated as "already
     awake" — the entry is gone from `waiters` → return
     `Ready(())`.
  5. **Cancellation:** `SleepFuture::Drop` acquires the lock
     and calls `waiters.remove(&waiter_id)` (no-op if the
     waker already fired). Dropping while holding no lock is
     safe because `Drop` acquires and releases the lock
     synchronously; polling and Drop of the same future
     cannot race (Rust ownership).
  6. **Wake step** — `FakeClock::advance(&self, delta)` and
     `advance_to(&self, target)`:
     - Under the lock: bump `now`; drain `wake_at <= now`
       entries out of `waiters` into a local `Vec<Waker>`
       stack variable.
     - **Release the lock BEFORE calling `waker.wake()`**
       (round-27 H6 "wake outside lock" invariant). This
       prevents deadlock if the woken future re-acquires the
       same mutex during its poll (Tokio's default `wake`
       shape polls immediately if the executor is the
       current thread's cooperative scheduler).
     - Wake in insertion order (BTreeMap preserves key
       order = waiter id order = registration order); this
       is deterministic across runs.
  7. **Overflow:** `advance` saturates on `Duration` overflow
     (`inner.now = inner.now.saturating_add(delta)`); wake
     step still runs. `sleep(Duration::MAX)` becomes an
     effectively-forever waiter — deterministic tests should
     `advance_to(Duration::MAX)` explicitly to drain.
  8. **`Clock::now_monotonic`** reads `inner.now` (a
     `std::time::Duration`) under the lock. **`Clock::now`
     converts + saturates** — round-30 H4: the round-29
     one-liner `wall.checked_add(inner.now)` did not
     type-check because `OffsetDateTime::checked_add` takes
     `time::Duration`, not `std::time::Duration`. Correct
     shape:
     ```rust
     fn now(&self) -> OffsetDateTime {
         // Round-32 auction core: replace `.expect("poisoned")` on the
         // mutex lock (production code can't call `.expect` under
         // the workspace restriction lint). `PoisonError` means
         // some other test panicked while holding the lock; we
         // recover the inner state via `into_inner()` and
         // continue — the value itself is fine, only the guard
         // was contaminated.
         let inner_now = match self.inner.lock() {
             Ok(guard) => guard.now,
             Err(poisoned) => poisoned.into_inner().now,
         };
         // Round-30 H4: three failure modes each saturate to
         // `OffsetDateTime::MAX_UTC`:
         //   (a) inner_now overflows time::Duration (its
         //       max is i64::MAX seconds while std's is u64::MAX);
         //   (b) checked_add itself overflows the datetime range;
         //   (c) already-max wall clock.
         let delta = match time::Duration::try_from(inner_now) {
             Ok(d) => d,
             Err(_) => return OffsetDateTime::MAX_UTC,
         };
         self.wall
             .checked_add(delta)
             .unwrap_or(OffsetDateTime::MAX_UTC)
     }
     ```
     The overflow test case
     `now_saturates_to_max_offset_datetime_after_advance_to_max()`
     locks in the behaviour, along with a matching
     `now_saturates_when_inner_exceeds_time_duration_range()`
     that constructs an inner_now of `u64::MAX` seconds
     directly to trigger the `try_from` failure path.

  Integration tests compile the library without `cfg(test)` set
  in the library itself, so a `#[cfg(test)] pub(crate) fn
waiters_len(&self)` accessor is NOT visible from a
  `tests/*.rs` integration binary. Two options in one:
  - Zero-, single-, two-waiter and cancellation cases live
    inside the crate's own test module where `cfg(test)` is
    truly on.
  - If any of the cases must be exercised from an INTEGRATION
    test binary later (e.g. combining Timer + a real Tokio

    guard AND the crate exposes `test-inspection` as a Cargo

    `cfg(test)` alone in a lib does not extend to callers.

- [ ] **Step 3 — Add `FanoutStrategy` trait + BOTH concrete
      types.** Round-32 B1 (was in Task 11; moved earlier so Task
      9.5's `ProductionFanout::send_all` rewrite compiles). File:
      `crates/auctioneer-core/src/host_primitives/strategy.rs`.

  ```rust
  use crate::host_primitives::ProxyClientApi;
  // Round-86 B5 — `TimeoutCause` at MODULE scope (the `RaceOutcome::
  // Timeout(TimeoutCause)` enum needs it, not just `drive_one`), and
  // `Duration` for the pre-expired guard / `elapsed` fields.
  use auctioneer_exchange::{AuctionDeadline, BidderCall, BidderCallResult, TimeoutCause};
  use auctioneer_runtime::{Clock, Timer};
  use std::time::Duration;

  #[async_trait::async_trait(?Send)]
  pub trait FanoutStrategy: Send + Sync {
      async fn drive_one<'a>(
          &'a self,
          client: &'a dyn ProxyClientApi,
          call: &'a BidderCall,
          deadline: &'a AuctionDeadline,
          clock: &'a dyn Clock,
          timer: &'a dyn Timer,
      ) -> BidderCallResult;
  }

  /// Explicit definition (round-35 B1 canonical, round-36 auction core
  /// dropped the generic parameter — was `RaceOutcome<T>`
  /// in one block and `RaceOutcome` in another). Consumed by
  /// `BiasedRace3<'_, RaceOutcome>` inside
  /// `RaceTimersStrategy::drive_one`. `Sent` carries
  /// `Result<BidderHttpResponse, ProxyError>` (round-48 Step 0 —
  /// the typed error introduced in GDPR fanout; matches
  /// `ProxyClientApi::send_one`'s new signature).
  pub enum RaceOutcome {
      Timeout(TimeoutCause),
      Sent(Result<auctioneer_bidder::BidderHttpResponse, auctioneer_bidder::ProxyError>),
  }

  /// GDPR fanout delegate: replicates the auction core DevFanout single-call
  /// path (gzip encode → send → classify). Never awaits the
  /// Timer, so an immediate-resolve stub is inert.
  pub struct DelegateToDevStrategy;

  #[async_trait::async_trait(?Send)]
  impl FanoutStrategy for DelegateToDevStrategy {
      async fn drive_one<'a>(
          &'a self,
          client: &'a dyn ProxyClientApi,
          call: &'a BidderCall,
          _deadline: &'a AuctionDeadline,
          clock: &'a dyn Clock,
          _timer: &'a dyn Timer,
      ) -> BidderCallResult {
          use crate::host_primitives::fanout::{classify, prepare_outbound_request};
          let start = clock.now_monotonic();
          // Round-57 B-i: `prepare_outbound_request` returns
          // `Result<_, FanoutError>` (gzip is fallible); a prep
          // failure is this bidder's error.
          let prepared = match prepare_outbound_request(call) {
              Ok(p) => p,
              Err(e) => {
                  let elapsed = clock.now_monotonic().saturating_sub(start);
                  return BidderCallResult { result: Err(e), elapsed };
              }
          };
          let outcome = client.send_one(&prepared).await;
          let elapsed = clock.now_monotonic().saturating_sub(start);
          BidderCallResult {
              // Round-35 B2: GDPR fanout keeps the auction core
              // `max_response_bytes` field. `max_transport_bytes`
              // / `max_decoded_bytes` migration lands in bounded fanout.
              result: classify(outcome, call.max_response_bytes),
              elapsed,
          }
      }
  }

  /// Axum-only real race strategy. **Lands with a working
  /// `impl FanoutStrategy` in Task 9.5** (round-35 B1: the
  /// round-33 "struct without impl" pattern broke Task 10
  /// compilation because Bucket B rows construct
  /// `ProductionFanout::new(..., Arc::new(RaceTimersStrategy))`
  /// even under `#[ignore]`). Cloudflare / Fastly / Spin
  /// install `DelegateToDevStrategy` at Task 9.5 commit
  /// time and continue running it through all of GDPR fanout; Task
  /// 11 Step 1 flips ONLY the Axum install to
  /// `Arc::new(RaceTimersStrategy)`. The impl is the same
  /// body Task 11 previously carried; consolidating here
  /// removes the duplicate spec.
  pub struct RaceTimersStrategy;

  #[async_trait::async_trait(?Send)]
  impl FanoutStrategy for RaceTimersStrategy {
      async fn drive_one<'a>(
          &'a self,
          client: &'a dyn ProxyClientApi,
          call: &'a BidderCall,
          deadline: &'a AuctionDeadline,
          clock: &'a dyn Clock,
          timer: &'a dyn Timer,
      ) -> BidderCallResult {
          use crate::host_primitives::fanout::{classify, prepare_outbound_request};
          use crate::host_primitives::race::BiasedRace3;
          // Round-54 B2: `TimeoutCause` and `FanoutError` are used
          // below (RaceOutcome::Timeout(TimeoutCause::…),
          // Err(FanoutError::Timeout(cause))) and must be imported.
          // `TimeoutCause` is re-exported from the auctioneer-exchange
          // root (see the migration inventory) alongside
          // `FanoutError`.
          use auctioneer_exchange::{FanoutError, TimeoutCause};
          use futures::FutureExt as _;

          let start = clock.now_monotonic();
          // Round-69 H2 — PRE-EXPIRED GUARD, before ANY work. If the
          // absolute auction deadline is already at/behind `now`,
          // short-circuit with the deadline timeout and do NOT compress
          // (`prepare_outbound_request`) or dispatch. The round-57 draft
          // ran gzip first and only measured the deadline afterward, so
          // a call handed an already-expired deadline still paid the
          // compression cost and (via the race) could still touch the
          // proxy. Guarding here makes "pre-expired" observably free.
          if deadline.deadline_at.saturating_sub(start) == Duration::ZERO {
              return BidderCallResult {
                  result: Err(FanoutError::Timeout(TimeoutCause::AuctionDeadline)),
                  elapsed: Duration::ZERO,
              };
          }
          // Round-57 B-i: `prepare_outbound_request` can fail (gzip
          // encoding is fallible), so it returns
          // `Result<_, FanoutError>` — a prep failure is a per-bidder
          // error, not a panic.
          let prepared = match prepare_outbound_request(call) {
              Ok(p) => p,
              Err(e) => {
                  let elapsed = clock.now_monotonic().saturating_sub(start);
                  return BidderCallResult { result: Err(e), elapsed };
              }
          };
          // Round-57 B-i: compute the ABSOLUTE-deadline remaining
          // AFTER prep. Measuring it at `start` (before gzip) and then
          // starting `deadline_arm` after prep would add the prep time
          // back onto the deadline, EXTENDING tmax past
          // `deadline.deadline_at` (spec §5.2 — the auction deadline is
          // absolute). Recompute against `now` right before the race.
          let deadline_remaining = deadline
              .deadline_at
              .saturating_sub(clock.now_monotonic());

          // Round-54 B3: pass the arms BY VALUE — `BiasedRace3::new`
          // boxes them (`Box::pin`), so no local `pin!` bindings are
          // needed and the losing futures drop with the race. Bias
          // order = bidder, deadline, send (bidder wins a tie).
          let bidder_arm = timer
              .sleep(call.timeout)
              .map(|()| RaceOutcome::Timeout(TimeoutCause::Bidder));
          let deadline_arm = timer
              .sleep(deadline_remaining)
              .map(|()| RaceOutcome::Timeout(TimeoutCause::AuctionDeadline));
          let send_arm = client
              .send_one(&prepared)
              .map(RaceOutcome::Sent);

          let outcome = BiasedRace3::new(bidder_arm, deadline_arm, send_arm).await;
          let elapsed = clock.now_monotonic().saturating_sub(start);
          match outcome {
              RaceOutcome::Timeout(cause) => BidderCallResult {
                  result: Err(FanoutError::Timeout(cause)),
                  elapsed,
              },
              RaceOutcome::Sent(sent) => BidderCallResult {
                  // Round-35 B2: auction core shape — `max_response_bytes`.
                  result: classify(sent, call.max_response_bytes),
                  elapsed,
              },
          }
      }
  }
  ```

  Note: `prepare_outbound_request` and `classify` are
  pub(crate) helpers extracted from `DevFanout::send_one` as
  part of this task (Step 3 delivers both `strategy.rs`,
  `race.rs`, and the helper extraction in one commit). Round-108 B2
  forward note (no GDPR fanout change): Fanout-2 RETIRES
  `prepare_outbound_request` — its gzip/entity-header work moves to
  `auctioneer_bidder::finalize_for_transport`, called by the exchange
  before `BidderCall` construction, and the drive then sends
  `call.request` as-is.
  **Round-57 B-i / round-58 B3: `prepare_outbound_request(call:
&BidderCall) -> Result<BidderHttpRequest, FanoutError>`** — the
  return type is **`BidderHttpRequest`** (the exact `&`-borrowed
  type `ProxyClientApi::send_one(&self, req: &BidderHttpRequest)`
  consumes at
  [fanout.rs:26](../../../crates/auctioneer-core/src/host_primitives/fanout.rs#L26));
  there is NO separate `PreparedRequest` type. gzip encoding is
  fallible, so the helper returns `Result` (a gzip failure becomes
  `FanoutError::Other(..)`); both strategy `drive_one`s early-return
  a `BidderCallResult { result: Err(e), .. }` on prep failure, and
  the `send_arm` calls `client.send_one(&prepared)` where `prepared:
BidderHttpRequest`. The auction core `DevFanout::send_one` that this is
  extracted from must be updated to propagate the same `Result` at
  its single call site.

  **`ProductionFanout::send_all` body (round-55 H1 — owned HERE,
  not Task 11).** The same commit rewrites `send_all` in
  `edgezero_proxy.rs` (already in this task's Modify list) to
  dispatch every call through the installed strategy and reassemble
  in call order:

  ```rust
  async fn send_all(
      &self,
      calls: Vec<BidderCall>,
      deadline: AuctionDeadline,
  ) -> Result<Vec<BidderCallResult>, FanoutInternalError> {
      // `join_all` preserves input order and yields `vec![]` for
      // empty input (Task 10 zero-calls conformance) with no
      // special-casing. Each `drive_one` is self-contained: under
      // `RaceTimersStrategy` it races its own timers internally;
      // under the installed `DelegateToDevStrategy` it is the auction core
      // single-call path, so overall behaviour is unchanged.
      let futures = calls.iter().map(|call| {
          self.strategy.drive_one(
              &self.adapter,  // round-57 B-h: the field is `adapter`
                              // (EdgeZeroProxyAdapter: ProxyClientApi),
                              // a value — NOT `&*self.proxy`
              call,
              &deadline,     // by-value arg (round-35 B4: no deadline
                             // field on the boot-time singleton)
              &*self.clock,
              &*self.timer,
          )
      });
      Ok(futures::future::join_all(futures).await)
  }
  ```

  `drive_one` never errors at the outer level — a per-bidder
  timeout is an `Err` inside `BidderCallResult.result`, so the
  outer `Result` is always `Ok` here (`FanoutInternalError` is
  reserved for a genuine orchestration fault). This is the ONLY
  `send_all` rewrite in the plan; Task 11 does not touch it.

deadline / per-call-timeout / mid-fanout-isolation tests against
`DevFanout` would fail-by-design. So the conformance suite splits
into two buckets:

`ProductionFanout`, 7 cases):** covers behavior that does not depend

  NOT map to `Unreachable` `(999, 103)`: GDPR fanout cannot distinguish
  unreachable from any other transport failure (`EdgeError` has no
  connect kind — round-49 B3), so the old
  `transport_error_yields_unreachable_code_999` expectation is
  impossible and is retired. Fine-grained `Unreachable`/`Timeout`
  classification returns with EdgeZero Prereq T. Runs against both

- `zero_calls_returns_empty_result_set`
- `single_call_success_returns_ok_and_elapsed_within_bounds`
- `transient_transport_errors_are_not_retried`
- **`results_preserve_input_order_when_calls_complete_out_of_order`**
  — `join_all` in `DevFanout` naturally preserves input order (the
  `BidderCallResult` vec is built from a `Vec<Future>` iterated in
  order), and Task 11's `ProductionFanout` explicit index-tagging +
  reassembly step must preserve the same guarantee per
  [fanout.rs:60](../../../crates/auctioneer-exchange/src/fanout.rs#L60) +
  spec §5.2:1088. Both sides participate.
- **`per_bidder_isolation_fast_bidder_elapsed_matches_own_delay`**
  — the `BidderFanout` contract only exposes the final

  [fanout.rs:60](../../../crates/auctioneer-exchange/src/fanout.rs#L60),
  so the earlier "surfaces while pending" phrasing was
  unobservable. Instead assert that `results[fast].elapsed`

  tolerance) even when a co-fanout-batch slow bidder waits much
  longer. Under `DevFanout` the `join_all` shape resolves futures
  concurrently, so the fast bidder's `elapsed` is bounded by its
  own delay — testable against both fanouts.

previous "3 cases" listing forgot the

(bidder-response decompression is deliberately NOT tested here —
the spec's gzip rules apply to outbound REQUEST compression and

  two mid-flight cases, else they HANG).** `Timer for FakeClock` (Task
  9.5) fires a pending `sleep` ONLY when something calls
  `clock.advance(..)`; a plain `block_on(send_all(..))` whose
  deadline/timeout is still in the future registers a waiter and PARKS
  FOREVER. **Only `pre_expired_deadline_at_send_all_entry_short_circuits`
  is EXEMPT** — its deadline is at/behind `now` at entry, so the
  pre-expired guard returns synchronously with no advance (that is
  exactly the guard it means to test). The mid-flight cases
  (`deadline_expires_mid_fanout_…`, `per_call_timeout_expires_…`) MUST
  drive the clock manually — the bidder arm is a `TestProxyClient` that
  never completes, so only the timer arm can resolve:

  ```rust
  use std::task::{Context, Poll};
  let waker = std::task::Waker::noop();
  let mut cx = Context::from_waker(&waker);
  let mut fut = Box::pin(fanout.send_all(calls, deadline));
  // 1. Poll to Pending: bidder arm pending, timer arm registers a waiter.
  assert!(fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx).is_pending());
  // 2. Advance the SHARED FakeClock past the deadline / per-call timeout.
  clock.advance(Duration::from_millis(/* past the wake instant */));
  // 3. Repoll (one repoll suffices under the noop waker):
  let results = match fut.as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
      Poll::Ready(r) => r,
      Poll::Pending => panic!("still pending after advance past deadline"),
  };
  ```

  Assert `TimeoutCause::AuctionDeadline` (deadline case) /
  `TimeoutCause::Bidder` (per-call case). **The bootstrap-factory tests
  (`axum_production_strategy_installs_the_racing_path()` and the round-68
  H4 test) that assert `Timeout(Bidder)` against a bidder slower than the
  deadline follow this SAME poll→advance→repoll protocol** — OR set the
  per-call timeout at/behind `now` so the timeout arm is elapsed at first
  poll and no advance is needed. Do NOT write them as bare `block_on`
  awaits.
  **Round-87 H7 — `equal_call_timeout_and_deadline_ties_to_bidder_cause`
  is NOT exempt and must NOT be pre-expired.** The point is the tie-break
  when the per-call timeout and the auction deadline fire at the SAME
  instant. Setting both at/behind `now` is WRONG: the pre-expired
  auction-deadline guard returns `AuctionDeadline` BEFORE the race even
  starts, so the bidder-first tie logic is never exercised (the test
  would pass for the wrong reason / assert the wrong cause). Instead set
  the per-call timeout AND the auction deadline to the SAME FUTURE
  instant `t`, poll once to `Pending` (both timer arms register waiters),
  then `clock.advance(t - now)` so BOTH fire on the same repoll, and
  assert the biased race resolves to `TimeoutCause::Bidder` (the
  documented tie-break in Task 9.5's `strategy.rs`). This exercises the
  real simultaneous-fire path, not the pre-expired guard.

  ```rust
  #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
  pub enum TimeoutCause {
      /// Per-call timeout hit — bidder-side. Maps to
      /// `ext.errors[<bidder>].code == 1`.
      Bidder,

      /// `ext.errors[<bidder>].code == 1` AND raises the
      /// global `ext.errors.prebid` code 12.
      AuctionDeadline,
  }

  pub enum FanoutError {
      Timeout(TimeoutCause),
      // ... existing variants ...
  }
  ```

  **Fixture design — round-28 C3 rework** (earlier draft mixed

  which cannot compile: once you hand a `TcpStream` to
  `hyper::server::conn::http1::Builder::serve_connection`, Hyper
  OWNS the read half). **Round-65 foundations — Approach A (raw `tokio` TCP)
  is CANONICAL and the only one implemented; the former "Approach B —
  Hyper `serve_connection`" is dropped, not merely un-chosen.** Two
  reasons beyond determinism: (i) handing the stream to Hyper's server
  means Hyper's state machine may swallow a half-close on some
  versions, which is exactly the signal the test needs to observe; and
  (ii) it pulls `hyper` + `hyper-util` server-side dev-deps that the
  raw-TCP fixture does not need (round-65 foundations dep trim). The rationale
  is retained here for the record; do NOT reintroduce a Hyper server
  in the fixture.

  **Approach A — raw TCP (the canonical fixture, no framework in the
  loop):** for each accepted `TcpStream`, read into a GROWING buffer
  until `\r\n\r\n` (end of request headers) appears. **Round-63 H3 /
  round-64 B1 — the bidder request is a POST, so there is a request
  BODY after the headers; the fixture MUST fully consume it before
  observing cancellation, but a SINGLE `read` can return the headers
  AND some-or-all of the body in one buffer.** So: keep the bytes
  already sitting AFTER `\r\n\r\n`, parse `Content-Length` from the
  header slice, and read only `content_length - already_buffered`
  MORE bytes (bounded, not a fresh `read_exact(content_length)` —
  that would block forever on bytes that already arrived, a
  DEADLOCK). Only THEN write the minimal response header block
  (`HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\ncontent-length: 500\r\n\r\n`) and start the
  single-byte peek race. Without draining the body, the first body
  byte reads as `Ok(1)` and is misclassified as `ContinuedReading`.
  Round-29 H3: `io::Error` doesn't destructure to its `ErrorKind`
  directly; go through `.kind()`.

  ```rust
  use std::io::ErrorKind;
  use tokio::io::AsyncReadExt;

  // Round-64 B1: read headers into a growing buffer; a single read
  // may already carry body bytes past `\r\n\r\n`.
  let mut buf = Vec::new();
  let header_end = loop {
      let mut chunk = [0u8; 1024];
      // Round-65 foundations: bound the header read with a timeout too, so a
      // client that connects and then stalls cannot hang the test.
      let n = tokio::time::timeout(
          std::time::Duration::from_secs(5),
          stream.read(&mut chunk),
      )
      .await
      .expect("request-header read timed out")
      .expect("read request");
      if n == 0 { break None; }               // closed before headers
      buf.extend_from_slice(&chunk[..n]);
      if let Some(p) = find_crlf_crlf(&buf) { break Some(p + 4); }
      assert!(buf.len() < 64 * 1024, "request headers too large");  // bounded
  };
  let Some(header_end) = header_end else {
      record(ConnOutcome::ClientDrop); return;
  };
  // Round-65 foundations: a MISSING / malformed Content-Length is not
  // silently treated as a zero-length body (which would leave the
  // real body bytes to leak into the peek race as a bogus
  // `ContinuedReading`). The fixture controls the client, so a valid
  // header is a hard invariant.
  let content_length = parse_content_length(&buf[..header_end])
      .expect("bidder POST must carry a valid Content-Length");
  // Body bytes ALREADY buffered with the headers — do NOT re-read them.
  let already = buf.len().saturating_sub(header_end);
  // Round-65 foundations: a client that already delivered MORE than
  // Content-Length is a protocol violation (or an unexpected pipelined
  // request). `saturating_sub` would clamp `remaining` to 0 and let
  // those extra bytes leak into the peek race below. Reject loudly
  // instead of silently accepting a partial/oversized frame.
  assert!(
      already <= content_length,
      "client sent {already} body bytes, exceeding Content-Length {content_length}",
  );
  let mut remaining = content_length.saturating_sub(already);
  while remaining > 0 {                        // read only the REMAINDER, bounded
      let mut chunk = vec![0u8; remaining.min(8192)];
      // Round-65 foundations: bound every body read with a timeout so a stalled
      // client cannot hang the test indefinitely.
      let n = tokio::time::timeout(
          std::time::Duration::from_secs(5),
          stream.read(&mut chunk),
      )
      .await
      .expect("request-body read timed out")
      .expect("read request body");
      // Round-65 foundations: n == 0 with `remaining > 0` means EOF MID-BODY —
      // the client dropped before sending the full request. That is
      // itself a client drop: record it and return. Do NOT `break` and
      // fall through to write a response as though the request had
      // completed (the round-64 draft did exactly that, reporting a
      // truncated request as a normal one).
      if n == 0 {
          record(ConnOutcome::ClientDrop);
          return;
      }
      remaining = remaining.saturating_sub(n);
  }
  // Body fully consumed (remaining == 0). The only further bytes are a
  // disconnect, so write the response and start the peek race.
  write_response_headers(&mut stream).await;

  let outcome = tokio::select! {
      _ = tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(500)) => {
          ConnOutcome::Responded
      }
      read = stream.read(&mut [0u8; 1]) => match read {
          Ok(0) => ConnOutcome::ClientDrop,
          Err(e) if matches!(
              e.kind(),
              ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof
              | ErrorKind::ConnectionReset
              | ErrorKind::BrokenPipe,
          ) => ConnOutcome::ClientDrop,
          // Round-63 H3: with the body already drained, a non-zero
          // read here is genuinely unexpected extra data, not the
          // request body — keep it as a distinct diagnostic.
          _ => ConnOutcome::ContinuedReading,
      }
  };
  ```

  Deterministic, no Hyper conflict.
  **Round-64 B1 — same-write regression:** add a fixture variant
  where the client sends the ENTIRE request (headers + full body) in
  a SINGLE `write` so the fixture's first `read` returns everything
  at once (`already == content_length`, `remaining == 0`). Assert
  the fixture does NOT block (it skips the body-remainder loop) and
  still reaches + reports the correct cancellation outcome — this is
  the exact interleaving the naïve `read_exact(content_length)` would
  have deadlocked on.

### Task 12: bidder-response cap — NO GDPR fanout code change (deferred to bounded fanout)

**Round-47 B1/B2 — Task 12 is a no-op in GDPR fanout; it defers to bounded fanout
in full.** The round-45/46 drafts tried to move the response cap
into the proxy read (`into_bytes_bounded(cap)` in `send_one`).
That is wrong for BOTH the memory reason (round-46 B1: the pinned
Axum adapter already buffered the whole body into a `Body::Once`
via `response.bytes().await`, so a read-time cap bounds nothing)
AND — round-47 B1 — the **wire-shape** reason:

- Oversize's correct bidder code is **4** (`seatnonbid.statuscode
= 100`). That mapping fires ONLY from `classify`'s `Ok(resp)`
  branch, which compares `resp.body.len() > max_response_bytes`
  post-buffer and returns `FanoutError::OversizeResponse` →
  `(4, 100)`
  ([fanout.rs:81](../../../crates/auctioneer-core/src/host_primitives/fanout.rs#L81),
  [run.rs:585](../../../crates/auctioneer-exchange/src/run.rs#L585)).
- If instead `send_one` reads with a smaller cap and
  `into_bytes_bounded` returns `Err`, that becomes
  `Result<_, String>` → `classify`'s `Err(msg)` branch →
  `FanoutError::Other` → **`(999, 100)`** — the WRONG code. Moving
  the cap into the read therefore _converts a clean oversize into
  a generic error_ and the proposed round-46 test (`assert (4,
100)`) could never pass.

So GDPR fanout leaves `send_one` exactly as it is
([edgezero_proxy.rs:74](../../../crates/auctioneer-core/src/host_primitives/edgezero_proxy.rs#L74)
reads `into_bytes_bounded(usize::MAX)`), and oversize is enforced
by the **existing post-buffer `classify(outcome,
call.max_response_bytes)`** — already correct auction core behavior, already
producing `(4, 100)`. On the buffered path `usize::MAX` costs
nothing: the adapter already materialised the whole body, so a
read-time cap could not lower peak memory anyway.

**Round-47 B2 — the cap stays exchange-owned; it is NOT added to
`BidderHttpRequest`.** `BidderHttpRequest` explicitly excludes
transport policy — its doc comment says so and points at
`BidderCall`
([types.rs:37](../../../crates/auctioneer-bidder/src/types.rs#L37)).
The single owner is `BidderCall.max_response_bytes`, which
`classify` already reads. GDPR fanout adds no field and changes no
signature.

**The typed proxy error is now in GDPR fanout** (round-48 follow-up —
Task 9.5 Step 0 introduces `ProxyError`, so `send_one` already
returns `Result<_, ProxyError>` and `classify` matches its
variant instead of substring-guessing).

**Round-49 H5 — how streaming oversize actually reaches
`(4, 100)`:** NOT through a proxy-error variant. bounded fanout's streaming
body yields a stream-item `Err(TypedBodyError::TooLarge)`, which
`classify_body_stream_error` maps to
`FanoutError::OversizeResponse { source: Transport | Decoded }`.
`ProxyError` has no `Oversize` variant precisely because nothing
would construct it (the round-48 claim to the contrary is
retired).

   `BidderCall.max_response_bytes` while `DevFanout::classify`
   still reads it (round-47 B2: the bounded fanout field-removal step is
   reconciled with this).

The peak-allocation regression (staged `cap + 10 MiB` behind a
real `Body::Stream`, asserting bounded peak + `(4, 100)`) is an
bounded fanout test (bounded fanout Task Fanout-7), not an GDPR fanout test.

  ```rust
              regs_gdpr: underlying.regs.as_ref().and_then(|r| r.gdpr),
              gpp_sid: underlying.regs.as_ref()

          ctx.account.config,
          ctx.host,
  ```

  signal helper the resolver uses internally). Task 8 Step 4
  adds a companion constructor

  that returns the allow-all context with pre-populated warnings.

  ```rust
  //    (Step 2). No alias registry needed here.
  let mut privacy = /* Step 2's non_standard_publishers branch */;
  // 2. HOIST the bookkeeping maps (round-68 B1). They MUST outlive the
  //    tmax check: the privacy live-filter (code 10017 + seatnonbid
  //    300) and the sampling sentinels below write into them BEFORE
  //    tmax is evaluated, and the tmax short-circuit AUGMENTS them
  //    rather than building fresh maps — so an already-expired tmax
  //    still returns the privacy/sampling bookkeeping, not just
  //    timeouts. (The round-67 draft wrongly let the helper own fresh
  //    maps AND evaluated the tmax check before `live` was declared —
  //    the round-68 B1 defects.)
  let mut bundles: BTreeMap<BidderName, BidderResultBundle> = BTreeMap::new();
  let mut seatnonbid: BTreeMap<BidderName, Vec<NonBidRow>> = BTreeMap::new();
  // 3. Alias resolution ran in the handler (Step 1a).
  //    `run_auction` reads `plan.aliases.map` — a `&AliasMap`,
  //    the exact type the auction core splitter + build_call_list already
  //    take (round-66 B3 — NOT `&plan.aliases`, a
  //    `&ResolvedAliases`, which those helpers do not accept).
  //    The plan is immutable for the auction's lifetime.
  let aliases = &plan.aliases.map;   // &AliasMap
  // 4. Split ONLY — round-69 B1: the max-bidders CAP is NOT here. It
  //    runs AFTER the privacy filter + sampling (step 6c below) so a
  //    sampled-out bidder FREES a cap slot instead of consuming one
  //    (acceptance §5.1 "sampled BEFORE the max-bidders cap" /
  //    round-22 H6). `split_by_bidder` is the auction core call (run.rs:59);
  //    there is no `split_and_cap` helper (round-66 B3). Round-106
  //    B4 / round-107 B4 (forward note — no GDPR fanout change): Fanout-2
  //    restructures this into DECIDE → MATERIALIZE → SCRUB:
  //    `group_by_bidder` (names + imp indices + ONE owned
  //    request_value, no clones), permission/sampling/cap decisions
  //    on names, `materialize_per_bidder` (typed clones for the
  //    post-cap survivor set only, FPD + code-15 here), then the
  //    step-6 scrubs applied to the materialized survivors per the
  //    recorded decisions — because full pre-cap materialization
  //    violates the bounded fanout memory envelope's max_bidders clone term.
  //    GDPR fanout keeps the auction core single-call shape + this step-6
  //    filter+scrub; per-bidder decisions and scrub outputs are
  //    identical either way (a snapshot test in Fanout-2 asserts it).

  let per_bidder = split.per_bidder;

  // per-imp disabled stream (both `Vec<(BidderName, ErrorEntry)>`;
  // empty in Task 13, populated by Task 16). Flows through the existing
  // `disabled_bidder_warnings` conveyor (run.rs:183+) unchanged.
  let mut disabled_bidder_warnings = split.disabled_bidder_warnings;
  disabled_bidder_warnings
      .extend(plan.aliases.disabled_warnings.iter().cloned());

  //    max-bidders cap (6c) run NEXT, IN THAT ORDER: they populate the
  //    hoisted maps and produce the fanout-eligible `capped` set. The
  //    tmax short-circuit (6e) is evaluated AFTER them (round-68 B1 +

  //    bookkeeping must exist first).
  // 6. Per-bidder privacy filter + SCRUB — populates the hoisted

  //    handed to fan-out. Activity / CCPA / GPP scrub rows stay privacy enforcement;
  //    only the two GDPR scrubs are in GDPR enforcement.
  //
  // Round-50 B4: resolve the IP keep-bits ONCE, before the closure.
  // `run_auction` reaches account config as `ctx.account.config`
  // (there is no bare `account` binding), and `IpKeepBits` is
  // `Copy`, so capturing this value keeps the closure free of any
  // `ctx` borrow.
  let keep_bits = ctx.account.config.ip_keep_bits();

      .into_iter()
      .filter_map(|mut p| {

  //     sampling (acceptance §5.1 / round-22 H6) so a sampled-out bidder

  //     misplaced it before the filter). `capped` is the fanout-eligible
  //     set; `bidder_cap_drops` feed the bookkeeping.
  let cap = ctx.host.resource_limits.max_bidders_per_auction.max(1);
  let (capped, bidder_cap_drops) = apply_max_bidders(live, cap);
  // 6d. Collect privacy warnings ONCE now that the filter has run
  //     (round-67 B2). Consumed by exactly one exit: the tmax
  //     short-circuit (moved BY VALUE) OR the normal path's
  //     `ResponseInput.prebid_warnings`.

  // 6e. tmax short-circuit — the EXISTING auction core resolve_tmax/remaining
  //     computation (run.rs:79-97; there is NO `ctx.tmax_effective()`).
  //     It runs AFTER filter + sampling + cap so `capped` and the
  //     hoisted maps are fully populated (round-68 B1 / round-69 B1).
  let req_tmax_ms = underlying.tmax.and_then(|t| u64::try_from(t).ok());
  let resolved_tmax = resolve_tmax(req_tmax_ms, ctx.host, ctx.request_start);
  let bidder_visible_tmax_ms = resolved_tmax.bidder_visible_tmax_ms;
  let deadline = resolved_tmax.deadline;
  let now = ctx.clock.now_monotonic();
  let remaining = deadline.deadline_at.saturating_sub(now);
  let auction_timestamp_ms = auction_timestamp(ctx);
  if remaining == Duration::ZERO {
      // AUGMENT the maps (round-68 B1). The helper folds the disabled +
      // cap-drop bookkeeping, then adds per-`capped`-bidder timeout
      // (code 1 + seatnonbid 101) via `.entry().or_default()`.
      // Privacy-denied bidders (10017 + nonbid 300) and sampled-out
      // sentinels are ALREADY in the maps and are preserved untouched
      // (a denied/sampled bidder is not in `capped`). Global code 12
      // (TmaxTimeout) goes on `ext.errors.prebid`, not nbr.
      // Round-69 B2 — `bundles`/`seatnonbid` are passed BY VALUE (moved);
      // `ResponseInput` OWNS both maps (response.rs), so the helper
      // cannot construct it from `&mut` borrows. Moving is safe: this
      // arm returns, so the caller never touches the maps afterward.
      return short_circuit_tmax_expired(
          &underlying,
          &capped,
          &disabled_bidder_warnings,
          &bidder_cap_drops,
          bundles,      // round-69 B2 — BY VALUE (moved into ResponseInput)
          seatnonbid,   // round-69 B2 — BY VALUE
          bidder_visible_tmax_ms,
          auction_timestamp_ms,
          ctx.features,
          prebid_warnings,   // round-67 B2
  ```

  **Ordering rationale (round-48 foundations — accurate about the split).**
  The spec (§5.1 step 6 privacy, step 7 aliases) orders privacy
  before aliases. GDPR fanout's executable order splits "privacy" into two
  parts that straddle alias resolution, and this is behaviorally
  equivalent because the two subsystems are INDEPENDENT (privacy
  inputs `regs.gdpr` / `user.consent` / `regs.gpp*` are
  request-level and do not depend on which bidders participate;
  alias resolution does not read any privacy state):
  1. **Privacy's only FATAL output runs FIRST**, before aliases —
     the precedence-aware `validate_wire_signal_input(&underlying)?`
     at handler Step 0 (invalid `regs.gdpr` → 400 per §7.1 rule 2).
     So the spec's "privacy before aliases" PRECEDENCE is honored
     where it is observable: a request that would both 400 on
     privacy (invalid `regs.gdpr`) AND 400 on an oversized
     `aliasgvlids` entry returns the privacy 400, because Step 0
     precedes `resolve_aliases` (Step 2).
  2. **`resolve_aliases` (Step 2)** runs next, at handler entry.
  3. **The full `PrivacyContext::resolve`** (TCF parse + per-bidder
     permissions + non-fatal syntax warnings) runs inside
     `run_auction`, AFTER alias resolution. It emits NO fatal error
     (malformed TCF/GPP is warn-and-continue per §7.7), so placing
     it after aliases changes no 400 outcome and no warning
     ordering the client can observe (privacy warnings and alias
     warnings target different scopes and are collected into the
     same buffer regardless of interleaving).
     The per-bidder privacy DECISION (via `privacy.permissions(core,
alias)`) and the two GDPR scrubs are then applied AFTER split, on
     each `PerBidderRequest`. This is a deliberate, documented
     deviation from the spec's step numbering, justified by
     independence + the Step-0 precedence guarantee — NOT the earlier
     (inaccurate) claim that the full resolver runs before aliases.
     The hoisted bookkeeping maps and the Step-0 fatal gate are the
     structural moves versus auction core;
     the split itself and its cap logic are unchanged. This mirrors
     the shape `fold_prefanout_bookkeeping` already uses for cap-drops
     and disabled-bidder warnings — same map, same fields — so the
     response builder needs no changes. `NonBidRow.statuscode = 300`
     matches Appendix G line 5612 for the privacy-drop path.

- [ ] **Step 3b: The two GDPR scrubs (round-48 B1).** Create
      `crates/auctioneer-exchange/src/scrub.rs` — the GDPR enforcement subset of the
      Appendix C.2 matrix. Only the two GDPR-driven rows land here;
      `scrub_user_fpd`, the CCPA `scrub_device_ids_ips_user_demo_ext`,
      LMT/COPPA, and `scrub_tid` stay privacy enforcement.
      **Round-49 B1 — written against the ACTUAL openrtb types.** The
      round-48 draft did not compile: `user.eids` is a `Vec<Eid>` (not
      an `Option`), and `Device` has only ONE typed id field (`ifa`) —
      `dpidsha1`/`dpidmd5`/`didsha1`/`didmd5`/`macsha1`/`macmd5` do not
      exist as fields; they land in the `#[serde(flatten)] other` map
      ([device.rs](../../../crates/auctioneer-openrtb/src/types/device.rs),
      [user.rs](../../../crates/auctioneer-openrtb/src/types/user.rs)).

  ```rust
  // crates/auctioneer-exchange/src/scrub.rs
  // Round-68 foundations — `BidRequest` is NOT re-exported at the
  // `auctioneer_openrtb` crate root (lib.rs re-exports only
  // `NormalizedBidRequest` et al.); the type lives at its module path.
  use auctioneer_openrtb::types::bid_request::BidRequest;
  use auctioneer_openrtb::types::device::Geo;
  // Round-68 foundations — `scrub_geo_and_device_ip` takes `keep_bits:
  // IpKeepBits` (Task 2's type in auctioneer-config); the import was
  // omitted.
  use auctioneer_config::types::IpKeepBits;

  /// Legacy device-id keys that arrive through `Device.other`
  /// (the flattened catch-all) because they have no typed field.
  const LEGACY_DEVICE_ID_KEYS: [&str; 6] = [
      "dpidsha1", "dpidmd5", "didsha1", "didmd5", "macsha1", "macmd5",
  ];

  /// Appendix C.2 `scrub_gdpr_id` — applied when GDPR `PassID=false`.
  /// Idempotent; safe on a request whose fields are already absent.
  pub(crate) fn scrub_gdpr_id(req: &mut BidRequest) {
      if let Some(user) = req.user.as_mut() {
          // User identifiers (see the spec-amendment note below).
          user.id = None;
          user.buyeruid = None;
          // User demographics.
          user.yob = None;
          user.gender = None;
          // EIDs in BOTH locations. `user.eids` is a Vec — `.clear()`,
          // not `= None` (round-49 B1).
          user.eids.clear();
          if let Some(ext) = user.ext.as_mut() {
              ext.eids = None;          // user.ext.eids: Option<Value>
          }
      }
      if let Some(device) = req.device.as_mut() {
          device.ifa = None;            // the only typed device id
          for key in LEGACY_DEVICE_ID_KEYS {
              device.other.remove(key); // the rest ride in `other`
          }
      }
  }

  /// Appendix C.2 `scrub_geo_and_device_ip` — applied when GDPR
  /// `PassGeo=false`. Rounds lat/lon to 2 decimals and masks the
  /// client IP to `keep_bits` via CIDR.
  pub(crate) fn scrub_geo_and_device_ip(req: &mut BidRequest, keep_bits: IpKeepBits) {
      if let Some(geo) = req.device.as_mut().and_then(|d| d.geo.as_mut()) {
          round_geo_2dp(geo);
      }
      // User geo too — it carries the same precision (round-49 foundations).
      if let Some(geo) = req.user.as_mut().and_then(|u| u.geo.as_mut()) {
          round_geo_2dp(geo);
      }
      if let Some(device) = req.device.as_mut() {
          // A malformed address is DROPPED, not passed through
          // unmasked (fail-closed on the privacy boundary).
          device.ip = device.ip.as_deref().and_then(|v4| mask_ipv4(v4, keep_bits.v4));
          device.ipv6 = device.ipv6.as_deref().and_then(|v6| mask_ipv6(v6, keep_bits.v6));
      }
  }

  /// Coarsen lat/lon to 2 decimals, HALF-UP (toward +∞) to match
  /// the spec's Appendix C.2 wording.
  ///
  /// **Round-51 auction core — parsed-`f64` half-up is the CANONICAL,
  /// documented semantic; there is no decimal-exact rounding.** The
  /// round-50 comment claimed a "DECIMAL-SCALED integer" but the
  /// implementation is ordinary binary `f64` arithmetic — the two
  /// disagreed. auctioneer receives `device.geo.lat/lon` already parsed
  /// into `f64` (the original decimal string is gone by the time
  /// the scrub runs), so decimal-exact rounding is not even
  /// possible without re-plumbing the parser. The privacy purpose —
  /// coarsening precise geo to ~1.1 km — is fully served by
  /// binary half-up, and the exact rounding direction at an
  /// unrepresentable half (e.g. `1.005`, which is `100.4999…`
  /// scaled and therefore rounds to `1.00`) is immaterial to that
  /// purpose. Tests therefore assert only FP-unambiguous values.
  fn round_geo_2dp(geo: &mut Geo) {
      geo.lat = geo.lat.map(round_half_up_2dp);
      geo.lon = geo.lon.map(round_half_up_2dp);
  }

  /// Half-UP at 2 decimals over parsed `f64`:
  /// `floor(v * 100 + 0.5) / 100`. Worked, FP-unambiguous examples:
  /// `1.238 → 1.24`, `1.232 → 1.23`, `-1.238 → -1.24`,
  /// `-1.232 → -1.23`. Non-finite input is returned unchanged — a
  /// NaN or infinite coordinate is malformed data the scrub must
  /// not convert into a bogus finite value.
  // Round-55 H2: `float_arithmetic` is a denied restriction lint,
  // but rounding a coordinate IS intentional float math and there
  // is no fixed-point coordinate type — `f64` is the wire
  // representation. `#[expect]` (not `#[allow]`) so the suppression
  // is flagged if the body ever stops doing float arithmetic.
  // `arithmetic_side_effects` does not fire here (it skips float).
  #[expect(
      clippy::float_arithmetic,
      reason = "intentional round-half-up on the f64 geo coordinate"
  )]
  fn round_half_up_2dp(value: f64) -> f64 {
      if !value.is_finite() {
          return value;
      }
      ((value * 100.0) + 0.5).floor() / 100.0
  }

  fn mask_ipv4(raw: &str, keep_bits: u8) -> Option<String> {
      let addr: std::net::Ipv4Addr = raw.parse().ok()?;
      let keep = keep_bits.min(32);
      // Round-55 H2: `checked_shl` returns `None` when the shift
      // reaches the bit width (i.e. keep == 0 → shift 32), which we
      // map to an all-zero mask — folding away the old `if keep == 0`
      // branch. `saturating_sub` + `u32::from` avoid the
      // `arithmetic_side_effects` / `as_conversions` restriction
      // lints; keep ∈ 1..=32 → shift ∈ 0..=31 → `Some`.
      let shift = 32_u32.saturating_sub(u32::from(keep));
      let mask: u32 = u32::MAX.checked_shl(shift).unwrap_or(0);
      Some(std::net::Ipv4Addr::from(u32::from(addr) & mask).to_string())
  }

  fn mask_ipv6(raw: &str, keep_bits: u8) -> Option<String> {
      let addr: std::net::Ipv6Addr = raw.parse().ok()?;
      let keep = keep_bits.min(128);
      // Round-55 H2: keep == 0 → shift 128 → `checked_shl` None → 0.
      let shift = 128_u32.saturating_sub(u32::from(keep));
      let mask: u128 = u128::MAX.checked_shl(shift).unwrap_or(0);
      Some(std::net::Ipv6Addr::from(u128::from(addr) & mask).to_string())
  }
  ```

  **Round-49 B1 — these helpers are NEW; auction core does NOT own them.**
  The round-48 claim that the auction core client-IP path already provides
  `round_geo_2dp` / `mask_ipv4` / `mask_ipv6` was wrong: auction core's
  `implicit_fill.rs` only _validates and selects_ a client IP
  (private/link-local rejection) — it performs no CIDR masking and
  no geo rounding. Both are implemented here for the first time.

  **`IpKeepBits` + `AccountPrivacyConfig` are defined and OWNED BY
  TASK 2 (round-53 B1).** The full concrete definition —
  `IpKeepBits`, `AccountPrivacyConfig`, `IpAnonConfig`, the
  `default_ipv4_anon`/`default_ipv6_anon` functions, the `impl
Default`, `AccountConfig.privacy`, `ip_keep_bits()`, the
  **`render_account_privacy` range checks (32/128) — round-58 auction core:
  range validation lives in the RENDERER
  (`RenderError::IpKeepBitsOutOfRange`), NOT `build_support.rs`; the
  one owner is the codegen renderer** — the
  `data/account-defaults.toml` block, the `codegen.rs` round-trip
  test, and the `(j)`/`(k)` build-failure cases — all live in Task
  2 (search Task 2 for "AccountPrivacyConfig is defined HERE"). This
  scrub task ONLY calls `account.ip_keep_bits()`. The former
  duplicate definition here is removed to prevent drift.

  **Round-49 H1 — SPEC AMENDMENT: `scrub_gdpr_id` also clears
  `user.id`, `user.buyeruid`, and the native 2.6 `user.eids`.** The
  spec's C.2 row summarises this scrub as "device ids, user
  demographics, `user.ext.eids`", which under-specifies it in two
  ways, so this is a deliberate, documented amendment rather than
  silent over-scrubbing:
  1. **2.6 / legacy eid parity.** The row predates native
     `user.eids` (OpenRTB 2.6). Clearing only the legacy
     `user.ext.eids` while leaving `user.eids` populated makes the
     scrub trivially bypassable by sending IDs in the 2.6 location.
     Both locations must be cleared or neither is meaningful.
  2. **`PassID=false` means no user identifier reaches the bidder.**
     Leaving `user.buyeruid` (a direct, bidder-scoped user id) or
     `user.id` would defeat the decision the gate just made.
     The spec's Appendix C.2 row and §3.1 field table are updated to

### Task 15: Host + account resolution from single-TOML `[gdpr]` / `[accounts.<id>]` (BEFORE `prepare()`)

**Deploy model:** auctioneer ships one config blob per deployment. The
same TOML that carries auction / bidder overrides ALSO carries
`[gdpr]` (host GDPR overlay) and `[accounts.<id>]` sections; there
is NO per-account or per-host key in the config store and no
async per-request store read. Publishers are compiled into the
deploy (or pushed via `auctioneer config push` as a single TOML
update, same mechanism as host tuning).

**Two-overlay flow.** `AuctioneerAppConfig` now carries BOTH a host
GDPR overlay AND the per-account map:

1. `AuctioneerAppConfig.gdpr: Option<HostGdprOverride>` — deployer's
   overrides on top of the baked `HostConfig.gdpr` from
   `data/host-defaults.toml`. Boot-time overlay onto the baked
   host default produces the effective `HostConfig` that
   `AuctionContext` sees.
2. `AuctioneerAppConfig.accounts: BTreeMap<String, AccountOverride>` —
   per-publisher overrides on top of the baked
   `AccountConfig` default. Boot-time overlay produces the
   effective `AccountConfig` for the request.

Without (1), enforcement literally cannot be enabled at runtime —
`Tcf2Config.enabled` and the per-purpose enforcement flags would
be stuck at their baked TOML defaults (which Task 2 also
introduces + defaults to disabled per spec §7.9). Task 19's
snapshot fixture uses the (1) overlay to turn enforcement on.

**Overlay semantics.** The `AccountOverride` → `AccountConfig`
overlay follows the same structural rules RFC 7396 defines — field-
level override with sibling preservation, whole-array replacement,
recursive merge for nested objects — but expressed as a typed-struct
`Option<T>` overlay rather than a JSON-value merge. Serde
deserialises the TOML into `AccountOverride`, then each
`Option::Some(_)` field replaces the corresponding baked default
field and each `Option::None` inherits it; nested maps
(`gdpr.purposes`, `gdpr.special_features`, `gdpr.channel_enabled`)
apply the same rule recursively per entry. This is semantically
identical to RFC 7396 for the fields GDPR enforcement exposes, with one difference
called out: **RFC 7396's `null → remove` case is unavailable** —
TOML has no `null` and serde `Option<T>` cannot distinguish
"explicitly null" from "absent". A field that is not set in
`[accounts.<id>]` inherits the baked default; there is no way in GDPR enforcement
to positively delete a defaulted field. The future config-store
account path can restore the null-removes semantics against the
JSON body it fetches.

  Fully synchronous — the `AuctioneerAppConfig` blob is already loaded at
  boot via the EdgeZero `AppConfig` extractor, so account resolution
  is a `BTreeMap` lookup, not a store round-trip. The resolver
  produces an owned merged `AccountConfig`.
  `ResolvedAccount<'a>` still borrows via `config: &'a AccountConfig`
  ([account.rs:11](../../../crates/auctioneer-exchange/src/account.rs#L11));
  the handler owns the `ResolvedAccountOwned` value on its stack and
  hands a `ResolvedAccount { config: &owned.config, ... }` down to
  `AuctionContext`.
- Consumes: new `AuctioneerAppConfig.gdpr: Option<HostGdprOverride>`
  AND `AuctioneerAppConfig.accounts: BTreeMap<String, AccountOverride>`
  fields added in Step 1 below.
- **Ordering guarantee**: account resolution runs BEFORE
  `auctioneer_openrtb::prepare()`. Two disjoint outcomes matter:
  - **Disabled account** (present in `AuctioneerAppConfig.accounts`
    with `disabled = true`): MUST surface `AccountDisabled`
    (HTTP 503) even when `prepare()` would also fail —
    account-side error wins.
  - **Unknown account** (publisher id present in the request but
    no matching `[accounts.<id>]` entry, OR no publisher id at
    all): NOT an error. Falls back to
    `AccountSource::DefaultFallback` with the baked default
    `AccountConfig`; `prepare()` then runs and surfaces any
    structural error as normal. This mirrors upstream's
    `PublisherUnknown` fallthrough (§9) — an operator that
    hasn't onboarded a publisher yet still gets 400s from
    structural request errors, not from account resolution.

  `MalformedAcct` (HTTP 500, code 10) stays in the taxonomy for
  the future config-store account path and is NOT emitted by
  GDPR enforcement's single-TOML resolver.

  The current handler calls `prepare` first
  ([auction.rs:87](../../../crates/auctioneer-core/src/handlers/auction.rs#L87));
  this task flips the order.
